Neonatal Cooper's hawks emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] with a hatchling wet weight of 22 grams [Wwb = 22 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial developmental mode characteristic of this accipiter. The age at hatching, recorded as 22 days [ab = 22 days] under those same incubation conditions, represents a relatively short embryonic period compared to other raptors of similar body mass at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Field observations consistently document this brief incubation interval, which is typical for temperate-zone accipitrids. The thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] at which these measurements were obtained corresponds closely to the average temperature maintained by incubating adult females in temperate forests, a microclimatic condition that balances embryonic development with the female's own energetic demands during the protracted courtship period.

The pronounced sexual size dimorphism exhibited by Accipiter cooperii is among the most extreme reported for any North American raptor. Adult females attain an ultimate body mass of 518 grams [Wwi = 518 grams], a value that exceeds the 342 grams [Wwi = 342 grams] recorded for adult males by over fifty percent. This substantial mass differential has been linked to differential prey selection and reduced competition between the sexes during the breeding season. Field studies indicate that female body mass can vary considerably across the species' geographic range, with individuals from northern latitudes often reaching masses toward the higher end of this spectrum. The considerable geographic variation reported in the literature suggests that local prey availability and winter severity may play significant roles in shaping ultimate adult mass.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period for this species (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), a predictable schedule of developmental milestones emerges for nestling Cooper's hawks. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching], a relatively abbreviated nestling phase that may reduce predation risk during the vulnerable chick stage at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The age at which gonadal maturation begins is considerably later, with puberty estimated to occur at 75 days after hatching [tp = 75 days after hatching] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This developmental delay reflects the substantial energetic investment required to complete the extensive somatic growth necessary before reproduction can be initiated. First-year birds are often still acquiring adult plumage at the time of pubertal onset.

First successful breeding in Cooper's hawks is typically deferred until 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching] when maintained at an environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a two-year delay that is consistent with the protracted period of territory establishment and courtship observed in many accipitrids. Reproductive output during this initial breeding event is comparatively modest: females produce a single clutch of 4 to 5 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 4 to 5 eggs per nest], and typically a single nesting attempt is made per year [F_R_i = single nesting attempt is made per year]. This low annual fecundity, coupled with the deferred age at first reproduction, constrains the species' intrinsic rate of population growth. The timing of first breeding is strongly influenced by local prey abundance, with birds in prey-rich areas sometimes breeding earlier in their second calendar year.

Maximum longevity records for Accipiter cooperii indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 20.3 years [am = approximately 20.3 years] in the wild, a lifespan measured at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] and representing one of the highest age estimates for any North American accipiter. This extended lifespan is likely facilitated by the species' generalist predatory habits and the low adult mortality typical of many forest-dwelling raptors. A detailed examination of banding recovery data reveals that senescent mortality increases notably after the fifteenth year, with very few birds exceeding two decades. The reproductive window, spanning from first breeding at approximately two years of age through the later stages of adulthood, allows for multiple breeding attempts that can partially compensate for the relatively small clutch size when averaged across an individual's lifetime.
